statement: Over her first $5$ games, a basketball player scored some average number of points per game. In game $6$ she scored enough points to raise her average by exactly $2$ points. In game $7$ she scored $10$ fewer points than in game $6$. Her average over all $7$ games was $15$ points per game. How many points did she score in game $6$?

choices.misconception: I found her average for the first $5$ games, $13$, and gave that instead of her game $6$ score.
I thought her game $6$ score had to equal her final average of $15$.

I thought raising the average of $5$ games by $2$ takes $2 \times 5 = 10$ points more than the old average, so I used $13 + 10 = 23$. But game $6$ must also be $2$ above the old average itself, so it needs $12$ more.
I thought the extra points had to raise the average of all $7$ games, so I added $2 \times 7 = 14$ to her old average of $13$ and got $27$.

hints: Let $m$ be her average for the first $5$ games. How many more points than $m$ must game $6$ be to raise the average by $2$?
Game $6$ must be $m + 2$ (the new average) plus $2$ extra for each of the $5$ earlier games, so it is $m + 12$. Then game $7$ is $m + 2$.

solutions.reliable: Let $m$ be the average of the first $5$ games and $x$ the game $6$ score. Raising the average by $2$ means $\frac{5m + x}{6} = m + 2$, so $x = m + 12$. Game $7$ is $x - 10 = m + 2$. The seven-game total is $5m + (m + 12) + (m + 2) = 7m + 14$, and it equals $7 \times 15 = 105$, so $m = 13$ and $x = 25$. Check: after $6$ games the average is $\frac{65 + 25}{6} = 15$, and game $7$ was $15$ points, so the average stays $15$.
solutions.elegant: Game $7$ scored $m + 2$, which is exactly the six-game average, so game $7$ does not change the average. So the six-game average was already $15$, which makes $m = 13$, and game $6$ was $m + 12 = 25$.
